{{Nihongo|'''Akira Hasegawa'''|長谷川 晃|Hasegawa Akira|4=17 June 1934 – 22 June 2025|lead=yes}} was a Japanese theoretical physicist and engineer who worked in the U.S. and Japan. He is known for his work in the derivation of the [[Hasegawa–Mima equation]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Mima|first2=Kunioki|date=1977|title=Stationary Spectrum of Strong Turbulence in Magnetized Nonuniform Plasma|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=39|issue=4|pages=205–208|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.39.205|bibcode=1977PhRvL..39..205H|issn=0031-9007}}</ref> which describes fundamental [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] turbulence and the consequent generation of zonal flow that controls [[plasma diffusion]]. Hasegawa also made the discovery of [[Soliton (optics)|optical soliton]]s<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Tappert|first2=Frederick|date=1973|title=Transmission of stationary nonlinear optical pulses in dispersive dielectric fibers. I. Anomalous dispersion|journal=Applied Physics Letters|volume=23|issue=3|pages=142–144|doi=10.1063/1.1654836|bibcode=1973ApPhL..23..142H|issn=0003-6951}}</ref> in [[glass fiber]]s, a concept that is essential for high speed [[optical communication]]s.

Hasegawa was the first to suggest the existence of [[Soliton (optics)|optical solitons]] in 1973. In 1974, he (together with [[Liu Chen (physicist)|Liu Chen]]) showed that plasmas could be heated with the kinetic [[Alfvén wave]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Liu|last2=Hasegawa|first2=Akira|date=1974|title=Plasma heating by spatial resonance of Alfvén wave|journal=The Physics of Fluids|volume=17|issue=7|pages=1399–1403|doi=10.1063/1.1694904|bibcode=1974PhFl...17.1399C|issn=0031-9171}}</ref> Hasegawa and Chen introduced the concept of the kinetic Alfven wave to illustrate the microscopic process of the [[Alfvén wave|Alfven wave]] heating.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Chen|first2=Lui|date=1975-08-11|title=Kinetic Process of Plasma Heating Due to Alfvén Wave Excitation|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=35|issue=6|pages=370–373|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.370|bibcode=1975PhRvL..35..370H}}</ref> In 1977, Hasegawa introduced the [[Hasegawa–Mima equation]] to describe turbulence in [[Tokamak|Tokamak plasmas]] and then further developed it in the 1980s (with Masahiro Wakatani) to obtain the Hasegawa–Wakatani equation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Wakatani|first2=Masahiro|date=1983|title=Plasma Edge Turbulence|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=50|issue=9|pages=682–686|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.50.682|bibcode=1983PhRvL..50..682H|issn=0031-9007}}</ref> The equation predicted an ''inverse cascade'' in the turbulent energy spectrum (i.e., from small to large wavelengths) and [[Zonal flow (plasma)|zonal flows]] (in the azimuthal direction in the Tokamak) that can control radial turbulent diffusion.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Maclennan|first2=Carol G.|last3=Kodama|first3=Yuji|date=1979|title=Nonlinear behavior and turbulence spectra of drift waves and Rossby waves|journal=Physics of Fluids|volume=22|issue=11|pages=2122|doi=10.1063/1.862504|bibcode=1979PhFl...22.2122H|issn=0031-9171}}</ref> With Wakatani, he wrote a paper on self-organized turbulence in plasmas.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Hasegawa|first1=Akira|last2=Wakatani|first2=Masahiro|date=1987|title=Self-organization of electrostatic turbulence in a cylindrical plasma|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=59|issue=14|pages=1581–1584|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.59.1581|pmid=10035273|bibcode=1987PhRvL..59.1581H|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

Hasegawa's proposal to trap plasmas with a dipole magnet similar to Earth's magnetic field, where turbulence caused by solar wind stabilizes the trap, was implemented in the first dipole plasma experiment<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Yoshida|first1=Zensho|last2=Ogawa|first2=Yuichi|last3=Morikawa|first3=Junji|last4=Watanabe|first4=Sho|last5=Yano|first5=Yoshihisa|last6=Mizumaki|first6=Shoichi|last7=Tosaka|first7=Taizo|last8=Ohtani|first8=Yasumi|last9=Hayakawa|first9=Atsuro|last10=Shibui|first10=Masanao|date=2006|title=First Plasma in the RT-1 Device|journal=Plasma and Fusion Research|volume=1|pages=008|doi=10.1585/pfr.1.008|bibcode=2006PFR.....1....8Y|issn=1880-6821|doi-access=free}}</ref> at University of Tokyo by Prof. Zensho Yoshida. In 2010, a [[Levitated dipole|plasma experiment with a floating dipole]] was also built at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Boxer|first1=A. C.|last2=Bergmann|first2=R.|last3=Ellsworth|first3=J. L.|last4=Garnier|first4=D. T.|last5=Kesner|first5=J.|last6=Mauel|first6=M. E.|last7=Woskov|first7=P.|date=2010|title=Turbulent inward pinch of plasma confined by a levitated dipole magnet|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nphys1510|journal=Nature Physics|language=en|volume=6|issue=3|pages=207–212|doi=10.1038/nphys1510|bibcode=2010NatPh...6..207B|issn=1745-2481|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Personal life and views==
Hasegawa was born on 17 June 1934, in [[Tokyo Prefecture (1868–1943)|Tokyo Prefecture]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nec.co.jp/press/ja/9509/1103-01.html|title=NEC: News Release 95/09/11-03-01|website=www.nec.co.jp|access-date=2020-02-20}}</ref> He was a graduate of the Department of Communications Engineering at the [[University of Osaka]], Japan and was a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] student at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he completed his Ph.D. under the supervision of Charles K. Birdsall in 1964. The title of his dissertation was ''Plasma Computer Simulation Using Sheet Current Model''.

He subsequently took a post doctoral position at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]] for six months, where he worked with [[Solomon J. Buchsbaum]]. Hasegawa was an associate professor in the Faculty of Engineering Science of the University of Osaka from 1964 to 1968. During this period, he served as a visiting professor at the Institute of Plasma Physics at [[Nagoya University]] and received the Doctor of Science Degree from the Department of Physics at Nagoya University.

Hasegawa rejoined Bell Laboratories in 1968, where he stayed as a distinguished member of technical staff until 1991. During his time at Bell Laboratories, he also became an adjunct professor in the Department of Applied Physics at [[Columbia University]] from 1971. He was a Distinguished Visiting Professor at the [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]] in 1980 as well as a visiting professor at the Institute of Laser Engineering at Osaka University. Hasegawa was elected as Chairman of the Division of Plasma Physics of  the [[American Physical Society]] in 1990, when he reported to the President the importance of [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]] research based on advanced fuels to avoid undesirable consequences of [[Deuterium fusion|deuterium tritium fusion]].  In 1991, he resigned from Bell Laboratories and transferred to the Faculty of Engineering at Osaka University. He retired in 1998.

In addition to over 250 scientific papers and several text books, Hasegawa published a number of books on the subjects of Japanese and [[Japanese Zen|Zen]] culture, which he learned from his spiritual teacher, [[Kobori Nanrei Sohaku]] of the [[Daitoku-ji]] temple. Following his retirement from Osaka University, he took a position as a lecturer at [[Kobe Women's University]] to teach a course on Happiness for Japanese Women, upon request of the founder of the university, Mrs. Kaname Yukiyoshi. He also worked as a professor at [[Himeji Dokkyo University]] and [[Kochi University of Technology]] and was a special consultant with [[Nippon Telegraph and Telephone|NTT Japan]] and [[BTG plc|BTG International]].

Akira Hasegawa was born to Japanese parents who were divorced when he was very young. He was primarily raised by his mother, Kaoru Takata, who was a graduate of Science and Mathematics Department in [[Nara Women's University]] His mother was a strong influence in developing his interest in mathematics. Hasegawa played on a baseball team while at [[Nagasaki|Nagasaka]] Junior High School. At Itami High School he was a member of the Science Club. While at Osaka University, he also played trombone in a Dixieland Jazz Band, which he and his friend formed.  He spent all of his scholarship money to purchase a large collection of jazz records, extending from [[Bix Beiderbecke]] to [[Miles Davis]].

In March 1961, prior to moving to the United States, Hasegawa was married to Miyoko.  Together, they have two sons, Tomohiro and Atsushi, and a daughter, Akiko. He played tennis but mostly enjoyed playing golf. Akira enjoyed being a member of the [[Rotary International|Rotary Club]] of Kyoto-East and publishing books on various non-science themes including history, finance, and culture. He believed that Japan is a country established on a unique matriarchal culture during the [[Jōmon period|Jomon period]], some ten thousands of years BC.

==Research activities==
Hasegawa made a number of seminal contributions in the subject of waves and turbulence in plasmas as well as in information transfer in [[optical fiber]]s. While at Bell Labs as a post doc, he succeeded in the theoretical explanation of a unique resonant phenomenon in magnetized plasma, referred to as the Buchsbaum–Hasegawa resonance.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Buchsbaum|first1=S. J.|last2=Hasegawa|first2=A.|date=1964-06-22|title=Excitation of Longitudinal Plasma Oscillations Near Electron Cyclotron Harmonics|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=12|issue=25|pages=685–688|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.12.685|bibcode=1964PhRvL..12..685B|issn=0031-9007}}</ref> While at the Faculty of Engineering Science Osaka University, he pioneered a computer simulation of plasmas in [[magnetic field]]s and supervised numerous students, including, Tetsuo Kamimura (Professor, [[Meijo University]]), Katsunobu Nishihara (Professor, [[Osaka University]]) and Hideo Okuda (Professor, [[Princeton University]]). Kiyoshi Yatsui (Professor, [[Nagaoka University of Technology]]) was an assistant in his group. During this period, he became acquainted with Professor Toshiya Taniuchi of [[Nagoya University]]. Professor Taniuchi then became a mentor of Hasegawa on nonlinear waves in plasmas and fluids.

In 1968, while at Bell Laboratories, Hasegawa joined a group in charge of [[Astrophysical plasma|space plasmas]]. His first theoretical work was to show that the observed oscillation on a satellite in the Earth's [[magnetosphere]] can be explained by an excitation of mirror instability coupled with a drift wave mode and named it the drift mirror instability.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hasegawa|first=Akira|date=1969|title=Drift Mirror Instability in the Magnetosphere|journal=Physics of Fluids|language=en|volume=12|issue=12|pages=2642|doi=10.1063/1.1692407|bibcode=1969PhFl...12.2642H}}</ref> This has become a pioneering work in space plasma instabilities. In 1973, while he was working on studies of the nonlinear evolution of [[Whistler (radio)|Whistler wave]] envelope, he discovered the same equation, the nonlinear [[Schrödinger equation]], applied to the envelope of [[Pulse generator|light pulses]] in glass fibers. With the help of [[computer simulation]] undertaken in collaboration with [[Fred Tappert]], he demonstrated transmission of a stable nonlinear optical pulse in fiber, which was later to be known as the optical soliton.<ref name=":1" /> The experimental verification of existence of the optical soliton was first made by L. F. Mollenauer et al of Bell Laboratories in 1980.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mollenauer|first1=L. F.|last2=Stolen|first2=R. H.|last3=Gordon|first3=J. P.|date=1980-09-29|title=Experimental Observation of Picosecond Pulse Narrowing and Solitons in Optical Fibers|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=45|issue=13|pages=1095–1098|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.1095|bibcode=1980PhRvL..45.1095M}}</ref> The nonlinear Schrödinger equation is now widely used for simulation of optical signal transfer in fibers over inter-continental distances<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hasegawa|first=A.|s2cid=26850330|date=2000|title=Soliton-based optical communications: an overview|journal=IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics|volume=6|issue=6|pages=1161–1172|doi=10.1109/2944.902164|bibcode=2000IJSTQ...6.1161H|issn=1077-260X}}</ref> and not solely limited to solitons.

Hasegawa and Liu Chen succeeded in explaining the Earth's magnetic oscillation mechanism (now known as the Chen–Hasegawa resonance<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Liu|last2=Hasegawa|first2=Akira|date=1974|title=A theory of long-period magnetic pulsations: 1. Steady state excitation of field line resonance|journal= Journal of Geophysical Research|language=en|volume=79|issue=7|pages=1024–1032|doi=10.1029/JA079i007p01024|bibcode=1974JGR....79.1024C|issn=2156-2202}}</ref>''')''' which was observed by his colleague, [[Louis J. Lanzerotti]]. This work also lead them to discover a new wave now called the kinetic [[Alfvén wave]]<ref name=":2" /> that resolved the [[Magnetohydrodynamics|magnetohydrodynamic]] singularity. A Bell Labs team of [[Clifford Surko|Cliff Surko]] (Professor at [[University of California, San Diego]]) and [[Richart E. Slusher]] ([[Georgia Tech]]) discovered low frequency plasma turbulence by laser scattering in the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory|Princeton plasma machine]]. Hasegawa with [[Kunioki Mima]] derived a two dimensional nonlinear wave equation that describes the observed turbulence spectra. This equation, now called the [[Hasegawa–Mima equation]],<ref name=":0" /> is widely used as the fundamental equation to describe low frequency plasma [[turbulence]]. One unique property of the equation is the existence of an inverse cascade of turbulent spectra which may form [[coherence (physics)|coherent]] structures such as zonal flow in the [[azimuth]]al direction in [[Cylinder|cylindrical]] plasmas.<ref name=":4" /> Hasegawa with Masahiro Wakatani extended the equation to the realistic geometry of plasmas confined in a [[toroid]]al magnetic field (Hasegawa–Wakatani equation) and demonstrated the universal excitation of zonal flow<ref name=":3" /> as the consequence of turbulence.<ref name=":5" /> To meet the needs of the high pressure confinement for advanced fusion fuel such as [[deuterium]]-[[helium-3]], in 1987 Hasegawa proposed<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hasegawa|first=Akira|date=1987|title=A dipole field fusion reactor|url=http://inis.iaea.org/Search/search.aspx?orig_q=RN:21025528|journal=Comments on Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion|language=en|volume=11|issue=3|pages=147–151|issn=0374-2806}}</ref> a plasma [[Thermonuclear fusion#Confinement in thermonuclear fusion|confinement]] by a [[dipole]] magnetic field generated by floating [[Superconductivity|superconducting]] ring current. [[Levitated dipole|Devices]] based on this idea were built at [[University of Tokyo]] by a research group headed by Professor Z. Yoshida<ref name=":6" /> and by [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and [[Columbia University]] team led by Professors J. Kesner and M.E. Mauel,<ref name=":7" /> and successful high pressure plasma confinements were demonstrated.

In September 1991, Hasegawa took a position of Professor of Communications Engineering in the Faculty of Engineering at [[Osaka University]] and started a new group of [[Fiber-optic communication|optical soliton based communication]] systems. He established international as well as domestic research groups that concentrated on ultra-high speed communications based on optical solitons. The group successfully demonstrated soliton based, all-optical ultra high speed communication over inter-continental distances. A student during this period, Toshihiko Hirooka now works as a professor at [[Tohoku University]].

After retirement, Hasegawa proposed two important concepts in [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]] devices. One is the idea that a fusion device operates as a power amplifier rather than as a reactor. Here, the device operates with the help of continuous injection of electromagnetic power that provides [[negentropy]] which maintains the desirable plasma pressure profile. The other is the concept of [[Chirality|chiral]] asymmetry of vortices generated in plasma turbulence where [[Vortex|vortices]] having positive (negative) core charge tends to expand (to shrink) which is essential in the formation of proper zonal flow for plasma confinement.

== Honors and awards ==
Hasegawa was a Fellow of IEEE and the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1975&unit_id=DPP&institution=Columbia+University|access-date=2020-02-20|website=American Physical Society|language=en}}</ref> Internationally, he was recognized as a recipient of the 1991 Rank Prize (British), 1995 Moet Hennessy, Louis Vuitton Da Vinci of Excellence Prize (French), 1999 IEEE/LEOS Quantum Electronics Award, and the 2000 [[James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics]] of the American Physical Society.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Hasegawa&first_nm=Akira&year=2000|title=2000 James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics Recipient|website=American Physical Society|language=en|access-date=2020-02-20}}</ref> In his citation, his innovative discoveries and fundamental contributions to the theory of turbulence of nonlinear [[drift waves]], the spread of [[Alfvén wave]]s in the laboratory and in space plasma, as well as [[Soliton (optics)|optical solitons]] and their application in [[telecommunication]]s were highlighted. He also shared with Kuniaki Mima and Pat Diamond the 2011 European Physical Society [[Hannes Alfvén Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.ucsd.edu/News/Story/174|title=UC San Diego {{!}} Patrick Diamond shares Hannes Alfvén Prize|website=physics.ucsd.edu|access-date=2020-02-20}}</ref>

Domestically, Hasegawa received several awards including, the 1996 C&C Prize, 1996 Achievement Prize of the Institute of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers (Japan), 1993 Shida Rinzaburo Prize (Japanese Ministry of Post and Telecommunications) and the 1995 Hattori (Seiko) Houkou Prize. He received the 2008 [[Japan Academy Prize (academics)|Japan Academy Prize]] and in 2010 The [[Order of the Sacred Treasure]], Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon from the [[Emperor of Japan|Japanese Emperor]].
